title: Scientists Put Caterpillars in an Ultraquiet Chamber to Learn How They Hear Without Ears
gist: Researchers used an anechoic chamber to show that tobacco hornworm caterpillars 'hear' approaching predators through supersensitive body hairs rather than ear-like membranes, a mechanism the authors say could inspire a new class of directional, air-particle-velocity-sensing microphones.

themes.theme: How caterpillars sense sound without ears

insights.claim: Tobacco hornworm caterpillars lack visible ears or tympanal membranes but can still detect approaching predators such as wasps, and ongoing research indicates they do this using tiny, supersensitive hairs on their bodies.
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: Identifies a previously unexplained biological sensing mechanism that researchers are now trying to translate into engineered acoustic sensors.
insights.quote: Our ongoing research suggests that tobacco hornworms can hear using tiny, supersensitive hairs on their body.

insights.claim: In anechoic-chamber trials, caterpillars continued reacting to airborne sound even at intensities below the threshold at which they responded to direct platform vibrations, indicating they were sensing the sound itself rather than just vibration transmitted through the surface they sat on.
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: Provides experimental evidence that the caterpillar's hearing is a true airborne-sound sense rather than an artifact of substrate vibration, strengthening the case that a distinct sensory organ is at work.
insights.quote: We noticed that this time the caterpillars continued reacting to the sound even beneath their threshold of response to the direct vibrations.
insights.locator: We noticed that this time the caterpillars

insights.claim: When researchers surgically removed specific hairs from caterpillars, the animals' defensive reactions to sound decreased dramatically across various frequencies depending on which hairs were removed, pointing to those hairs as the caterpillars' functional 'ears.'
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: A causal experiment (removal reduces response) is stronger evidence than correlation alone, giving the hair-based hearing hypothesis real empirical weight.
insights.quote: The caterpillars’ defensive reactions decreased dramatically across various sound frequencies depending on which specific hairs were removed.

insights.claim: The researchers' findings on caterpillar hearing have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, and the work is described as still ongoing.
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: Flags that the underlying science is preliminary and unpublished, so any downstream technology claims remain speculative for now.
insights.quote: While our research continues, and we haven’t yet published our results in a journal, this work is allowing us to piece together the caterpillar hearing puzzle

insights.claim: Standard microphones use membranes to detect sound pressure, but mimicking the caterpillar's hair-based sensing could allow future microphones to also measure air particle velocity caused by sound, not just pressure.
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: Suggests a concrete engineering pathway (bio-inspired velocity sensing) that could differentiate next-generation microphone or hearing-aid hardware, though it remains an early-stage research direction rather than a product.
insights.quote: future microphones could be designed to instead measure the air particle velocity caused by sound, alongside the sound pressure levels.
insights.locator: This line of research into how insects hear

insights.claim: A microphone able to track both sound pressure and air particle velocity could determine the direction a sound originated from, which the researchers say could benefit hearing-aid design by conveying both volume and direction to the user.
insights.speaker: Aishwarya Sriram
insights.so_what: Points to a specific downstream application (directional hearing aids) that would be the eventual commercial payoff if this biology-to-hardware translation succeeds.
insights.quote: Microphones that can detect air particle velocity would also be able to determine the direction of origin of the sound wave.
insights.locator: Microphones that can detect air particle velocity
